See Sharh, p. 453, where Mollâ Sadrâ quotes Chapter 155 of Ibn 'Arabî's Kitâb al-Fotûhât al-Makkîya. This is one of the clearest instances of Ibn 'Arabî's profound, hidden agreement with Shiite thought. The couplets introducing that chapter do nothing less than reproduce—without saying so—the teaching of traditions from the Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth Imams. The very idea that prophecy continues under the name walâyat cannot deny its Shiite origins. Then comes the rupture: the teachings about the Shiite Imams are made to disappear, at least apparently. Here lies a large part of the problem of Sufism. We shall see below how deeply Haydar Âmolî was troubled by this. On walâyat and wilâyat, see n. 20 above. ↩

The texts examined in the following pages belong to Haydar Âmolî's great Jâmi' al-Asrâr, published together with another of his books under the title La Philosophie shî'ite (above, p. 56, n. 29). Our general reference for what follows is Book III, fifth qâ'ida (principle), pp. 379–395. ↩

On prophecy beginning “in Heaven” with the da'wat (proclamation, or kerygma) of the First Intelligence of the Pleroma, see our Trilogie ismaélienne, pp. 141, 150 ff., and 162. The same idea appears in a fifteenth-century Twelver Shiite theosopher, 'Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. in Herat, 830/1427), in a short work used by the author of the seventeenth-century Dabestân. There this understanding of prophecy is attributed to the Ishrâqîyûn, the school of Suhrawardî. See vol. III, Book IV, Chapter III below. ↩

Here Ibn 'Arabî adopts a position that appears profoundly mistaken to Haydar Âmolî and to all Shiites. His entire teaching on prophecy and walâyat proceeds from Shiite premises (above, p. 250, n. 234). Yet he maintains that the Seal of absolute, universal walâyat is not the First Imam but Jesus. As for the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat, it would be Ibn 'Arabî himself. (On this latter point, we suspect that his commentator Dâwûd Qaysarî exaggerated the importance of a famous dream by transferring it to the plane of sacred history.) It would therefore be worth studying how the commentators on the Fosûs take positions on this issue. Haydar Âmolî holds Ibn 'Arabî in immense, admiring respect—he wrote his own commentary on the Fosûs—but cannot compromise on this point. Ibn 'Arabî's thesis breaks apart the whole understanding of prophecy: a Messenger who came before the Seal of prophecy cannot be made the “Seal of walâyat.” An entire chapter of Book II of Jâmi' al-Asrâr (pp. 355–448 of our edition) is devoted to refuting Ibn 'Arabî through theological tradition, philosophy, and theosophy. Haydar Âmolî returns at length to the issue in the introduction to his commentary on the Fosûs. We cannot explore this dispute in detail here, although it deserves close analysis. It shows precisely where Shiism recognizes something of its own in Ibn 'Arabî, and where it has to part company with him, for reasons reaching back to the still rather obscure early relationship between Shiism and Sufism. An anonymous annotator (p. 443, note) suspects a case of taqîyeh (prudential concealment of belief) on Ibn 'Arabî's part: “I have often observed,” he says, “that mystics use the name Jesus while meaning the Holy Spirit and the res divina [divine reality]; both refer to the Commander of the Faithful [the First Imam].” Ibn 'Arabî's apparent “error” thus highlights the relationship between the teaching about the Imams and the understanding of Christ. We shall discuss it again below, vol. III, Book IV, Chapter I. ↩

The number fourteen thousand is surely not accidental here. Just as, in Ismaili gnosis, the procession of the Seven divine Words or Cherubim during the heavenly Adam's “stupefaction” determines the sevenfold rhythm of the cycles of redemption (see Trilogie ismaélienne, index under “sept”), so here the number fourteen expresses the “pleromatic time” in which the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” proceed into being. ↩

This is what it means to call 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib the Seal of universal walâyat: of the walâyat belonging to all prophetic religions, just as Mohammad is the Seal of the prophets. Hence those extraordinary texts in which the speaker is not an Imam limited to a particular historical period, but an eternal Imam: “I am the gnosis of mysteries. I am the Threshold of thresholds … I am the Face of God. I am the one called Elijah in the Gospel … I am the one who holds the secret of God's Messenger” (Khotbat al-Bayân, above, n. 64). ↩

The name Owaysî comes from Oways al-Qaranî, a devout ascetic from Yemen. He knew the Prophet and was known to him although they never met in their lifetimes. He was one of the first Shiite martyrs (31/657). See our book on Ibn 'Arabî (above, p. 184, n. 149), pp. 26 ff., 29, 41, 45 ff., and 49. Among the great Iranian Sufis known as Owaysîs—those guided spiritually without physically meeting their guide—was Abû'l-Hasan Kharraqânî (d. 425/1034), whose guide was the spiritual being, or angel (rûhânîya), of Abû Yazîd Bastâmî. Another was 'Attâr of Nishapur (around 617/1220), guided by the angel or being of light of Hallâj. The same spiritual phenomenon appears in Arabic Hermeticism as the “Perfect Nature,” the philosopher's guide or “angel.” See the pages on the subject in Suhrawardî's work, below, vol. II, Book II. ↩

Haydar Âmolî, like Mollâ Sadrâ above (n. 232), refers here to Sa'doddîn Hamûyeh's Kitâb al-Mahbûb, in which Hamûyeh declares: “It is not permissible to use the name walî, either generally or in its specific meaning, for anyone after God's Messenger except 'Alî and his [eleven] descendants” (op. cit., p. 431). Sunni Sufism thus brings about a kind of secularization of walâyat. Sa'doddîn Hamûyeh (or Hamûyî) was a pupil and one of the kholafâ' (successors) of Najmoddîn Kobrâ. He taught 'Azîz Nasafî, was a friend of Sadr oddîn Qonawî, and corresponded with Ibn 'Arabî. After travelling for twenty-five years through Syria, Iraq, and Khwarezm, he settled in his native Khorasan, where he died in 650/1252. See Rayhânat, II, p. 193, no. 409. As already noted, he was distinguished by his personal relationship with the Twelfth Imam. In Haydar Âmolî's view, Dâwûd Qaysarî bears the chief responsibility for distorting Ibn 'Arabî's teaching about the person of the Mahdî. (Other commentators, Kamâl Kâshânî for example, have no doubt that the Seal of the Muhammadan Friends of God [Awliyâ], the Twelfth Imam, is the Mahdî.) Dâwûd so confuses the issue that it is no longer clear whether he means the Seal of universal walâyat or of Muhammadan walâyat. Haydar judges him harshly: “If Dâwûd Qaysarî opposes the eminent masters [mashâyekh], even his own shaykh and teacher, he does so only as a display of Sunnism [tasannon] combined with Sufism, to raise his standing in the eyes of the multitude” (op. cit., p. 436). ↩

At the beginning of § 2, we saw that, in Mollâ Sadrâ's account of knowledge, the outward sciences—the canonical sciences of revealed religious teachings—remain outside the “spiritual sciences,” which draw directly from the Giver of those teachings. ↩

Mollâ Sadrâ (Sharh, p. 453) offers a subtly ironic passage, still relevant today, contrasting worldly scholars and the officially recognized sciences ('olûm rasmîya) with those who know the realities of the other world and possess spiritual knowledge. Spiritual sciences cannot be approached by “anyone lacking the faculty to taste them [dhawq], however intelligent or experienced that person may be […]. Someone who has tasted them cannot make them known to someone who has never tasted them. One sign of the higher rank of spiritual sciences and of the scholars of the other world is that it is entirely possible to acquire other kinds of knowledge while loving this world and betraying the essential realities of pure religious feeling. Love of this world may even help someone acquire them […]. Scholars then undergo all sorts of difficulties because they know that gaining knowledge [bi-hosûl al-'ilm] will advance their careers and social standing [rif'a]. Spiritual sciences, by contrast, cannot coexist with worldly ambitions. They are revealed only when one sets passions aside, resolutely avoids the company of people intent on keeping up with their age, and shuns their easy or corrupt ways to devote oneself entirely to the spiritual life.” On Mollâ Sadrâ's personal ethics, see also vol. IV, Book V, Chapter II below. ↩

When Imam Rezâ was asked about this vision of the Prophet, his reply already anticipated that of Ibn 'Arabî and the mystics (see above, p. 227, n. 201), interpreting the age of the figure seen in the vision in relation to Mohammad's own age. Haydar Âmolî explains: “In reality, Mohammad saw only the form of his own soul, the most beautiful of Forms outwardly and inwardly … God created Adam in the image of his own form … Yet the Verus Adam [Adam haqîqî, the True Adam] is precisely the Prophet's eternal essence [haqîqat]. He saw it in the form of all its manifestations [mazâhir] as one single form, for the world is a Homo maximus [insân kabîr, the Great Human Being].” An anonymous commentator adds in the margin: “The Prophet's haqîqat—his Spirit, his Light, his soul, and his principle [asl], the Spirit of spirits, the reality of realities—is the Imam. There is an unsurprising convergence between Ismaili interpretation of the “Night of Destiny” (Qur'an 97:1–5) and that of Twelver Shiism. This is the hidden meaning of Imam Hasan 'Askarî's instruction to his aunt Hakîma to recite over the Child (the Twelfth Imam) the Qur'anic verse (97:1): “We sent it down on the Night of Destiny.” See also vol. Lâhîjî, Mafâtîh, p. 331. Here we touch on the theme of the enduring mystical hierarchies; see Chapter III, § 4 above. Curiously, one Sufi tradition found a compromise by making the Twelfth Imam the spiritual Pole of his own time, but then giving him successors in a “dynasty” of spiritual Poles beginning with his concealment. The author of Tarâ'iq al-Haqâ'iq (I, p. 258) even names the leading Sufi shaykhs in this “dynasty,” drawing on 'Alâoddawleh Semnânî's Kitâb al-'orwat al-wothqâ (on Semnânî, see vol. III, Book IV, Chapter IV). This is a point of tension between Shiism and Sufism. It fails to grasp what is meant by the Twelfth Imam's presence in both past and future, his time lying “between times,” between the past and what is to come. No one can therefore “succeed” the Twelfth Imam or even publicly “represent” him. Because he is concealed, his Bâb (“Gate” or threshold) is also concealed. From the Shiite perspective, anyone claiming such a status must be betraying the truth or acting as an impostor. ↩

Mollâ Sadrâ refers to those who have tried to evade the question of the succession of Imams by claiming that the “twelve” foretold by the Prophet were the first twelve caliphs, including the Umayyads. He shows the absurdities to which this thesis leads. He quotes the hadîth of the Prophet's nightmare (above, n. 22), in which he saw a band of monkeys climbing his pulpit and forcing the faithful to retreat. He calls on the commentaries as witnesses—those of Sunni authors such as Zamakhsharî, Fakhr Râzî, and Taftazânî, as well as that of the Shiite theologian Abû 'Alî Tabarsî. Finally he summarizes the introduction to Shahrastânî's Kitâb al-milal, in which Shahrastânî analyses the first dispute to shake the Islamic religion. Shahrastânî traces it back to Iblîs's revolt against Adam's investiture. That revolt spread through creation in seven successive disputes. They are mentioned in the commentary on the four Gospels (sic) and in the Torah (in fact the apocryphal Vita Adae et Evae, Life of Adam and Eve), and all were brought together in the form of manifestation (mazhar) taken by the first dispute in Islam. Shahrastânî, a Sunni scholar, is sufficiently allusive that a Shiite thinker like Sadrâ can invoke his text. Sadrâ ends this long discussion by quoting the Prophet: “Rulers will come after me. Those who gather around them, accept their falsehoods, and support their violence do not belong to me, nor do I belong to them. But those who refuse to take their side and refuse to accept their falsehoods belong to me, and I belong to them.” Sadrâ then shows that the numerous authentic reports (riwâyât) can refer only to the succession of the Twelve Immaculate Ones, with no other spiritual interpretation (ta'wîl) possible: those who know God and His Signs through mystical unveiling (kashf) and visionary witnessing (shohûd). The succession of the Imamate is unbroken. It perpetuates the line begun with Noah and Abraham, because the Imamate has the same essence as prophecy, of which it is the inward reality. The spiritual meaning of prophecy must endure. The saying must prove true: “Whoever dies without knowing the Imam of his time dies the death of those who remain unaware.” How could anyone dare maintain that this spiritual meaning and this knowledge have anything to do with one of the rulers the Prophet glimpsed in his nightmare? Sharh, pp. 462–464. III, Book IV, Chapter I), we shall quote a vision of Haydar Âmolî in which he perceived fourteen symbolic circles of lapis lazuli, with golden inscriptions, in the sky above Baghdad. See also, in our Trilogie Ismaélienne, the themes of the Imam as the “Soul of the soul” and the olive tree on the summit of mystical Sinai. ↩

Sharh, p. 475. Mollâ Sadrâ fully understands that he is opening a new way of spiritual interpretation for the philosopher to contemplate: “Make the most of all this,” he writes, “for you will find it in no book other than this one.” ↩

This extensive commentary on the ninth hadîth of Chapter VII thus follows the structure of the hadîth itself: the Imams are the A'râf, the Heights, and they are the pure springs (see above, p. 311, n. 301), opposed to the muddy springs. ↩

Ibid., Chapter VII, eleventh hadîth (from the Sixth Imam); Sharh, p. 476: “Just as the Hojjat [the guarantor or witness] is twofold, outward and inward, so too is wisdom twofold. There is a veiled wisdom and an unveiled wisdom. Veiled wisdom is what lives within the hearts of the prophets and the Friends of God [Awliyâ], the theosophers [hokamâ' ilâhîyûn, sages of divine wisdom]. Each of them is a sage in one respect, and wisdom itself in another.” This accords with what we have established about the unity of understanding ('aql), what is understood (ma'qûl), and the one who understands ('âqil). In the “metaphysics of witnessing,” that unity becomes the unity of testimony (shahâdat), witness (shâhid), and what is witnessed (mashhûd). See also below, p. 318, nn. 311 and 313. ↩
On the “inner Guide,” the Messenger of the inner world, and inner prophecy, see Sharh, p. 456 (commentary on Chapter IV, first hadîth). ↩

See ibid., Chapter VII, tenth hadîth (from the Fifth Imam). Mollâ Sadrâ's entire commentary could be studied as a gradual approach to the hidden Hojjat, an encounter with the inward Guide or Imam. He returns to the theme whenever the Imams' sayings invite him to. We shall briefly note some stages for future research. (1) Chapter IV, first hadîth (above, n. 309). (2) Chapter VI, third hadîth, Sharh, p. 465: a human being begins as little more than an upright biped. Then the soul slowly awakens from unawareness through a twofold Guide: the outward Messenger, who may be a nabî (prophet) or someone acting in his place; and the inner Imam (Imâm dâkhilî, Hojjat bâtina). (3) Chapter VII, seventh hadîth, Sharh, p. 472: the Sixth Imam's saying that “for every science God has established a door.” Only the person who knows that door knows the science: there is an outward door and an inward, esoteric door. Similarly, God's Hojjat is twofold, an inner witness and an outer witness. The first belongs to prophets and those like them; the second to ordinary people. (4) Ibid., eighth hadîth, Sharh, p. 472. (5) Ibid., eleventh hadîth, Sharh, p. 476 (above, p. 316, n. 308). (6) Ibid., thirteenth hadîth, Sharh, p. 476 (below, p. 318, n. 311): the outward Imam initiates the believer into the inward Imam; knowledge of the Imam initiates one into self-knowledge. This sums up Imami spirituality. (7) Chapter VIII, seventeenth hadîth, Sharh, p. 484: there is the door of the heart and the door of outward hearing; see also below, pp. 319 ff., nn. 314 and 315. (8) Sharh, pp. 484–485: in the long introduction to Chapter IX of Book VII, Mollâ Sadrâ examines witness and testimony and establishes the foundations for an Imami metaphysics as a “metaphysics of witnessing” (below, § 3 and p. 323, n. 324). (9) Chapter IX, second hadîth, Sharh, p. 485: the Imam as both outward and inward Witness. (10) Chapter XI, first hadîth, Sharh, p. 491: the Imams are both the Keepers of the Treasure and the Treasure itself; and so on. ↩

Chapter VII, eleventh hadîth, Sharh, p. 476; see n. 308 above. Veiled wisdom is the wisdom within the hearts of God's sages, the theosophers. “Unveiled wisdom, by contrast, consists of their very persons, for they are wisdom embodied [ashkhâs al-hikmat]. Whoever sees one of them sees the form and person of wisdom. It is for this reason that wisdom is given to them as a gift of immense good on behalf of humanity at large. For whoever knows his Imam and pledges allegiance to him pledges allegiance to God, and receives wisdom and an immense good—that is, the Imam himself, because the Imam is wisdom in person.” ↩
Ibid., pp. 476–477, commentary on the eleventh and thirteenth hadîth. ↩

Mollâ Sadrâ speaks of this union—a teaching also found in al-Fârâbî—as an event in his own inner life, an inspiration whose date he carefully recorded: sunrise on Friday, 7 Jomadâ I, 1037 AH (= 14 January 1628). See our introduction to Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques, pp. 2 ff., 185 ff., and the index under “ittihâd”; see also n. 308 above. ↩

Ibid., thirteenth hadîth, Sharh, p. 481: “In relation to the Second Life, human beings fall into two groups: the dead and the living. Among the living are those whose life is essential and personal, and those whose life follows from the life of another.” The Imam is the one who possesses essential life, infused directly by God. Yet through ittihâd (union; see above, pp. 316 ff., nn. 308 and 313) as it flowers into spiritual experience, whoever attains complete knowledge of the Imam thereby reaches the level of the Imam's inner light; that light becomes, in turn, the believer's own inner light. See also below, p. 323, n. 324, and the seventeenth hadîth, Sharh, p. 484, which recalls three groups of human beings: the 'âlim (the initiator, the sage), who is the Imam; the mota'allimûn, those who receive wisdom from the sage—the Imam's disciples or initiates; and, alas, the foam swept away by the torrent (ghothâ). Or, in Qur'anic terms: those brought close to God (moqarrabûn), the companions of the right, and the companions of the left. ↩

Ibid. On the unity of prophetic religion across successive periods, see also Chapter IX, first and second hadîth, Sharh, p. 485: “The Witness belonging to each community of prophets and Messengers—all the Witnesses [shohadâ]—is part of us [the Imams] and of our own company: members of the Family of prophecy and certainty, of direct witnessing [shohûd] and knowledge. They and we together constitute, in the true sense, the community of Mohammad. All the others who follow them also belong to Mohammad's community. Thus we and they are witnesses for the peoples and their followers, and Mohammad is witness for us. That is the meaning of Qur'an 4:45. Therefore, my friend, you must not reinterpret the Imam's words to make this verse refer exclusively to Mohammad's community, excluding the other prophets and their respective communities.” In understanding Mohammad's community this way, Mollâ Sadrâ gave voice to a Shiite “ecumenism,” an embracing of the unity of prophetic religion. Moreover, in the second hadîth of this Chapter IX, Imam Ja'far states that the Imams were expressly named in the holy Books revealed earlier, beginning with Abraham's Book (Sharh, p. 486). ↩
